title: Who are the barbarians?
hook: Montaigne asks whether the peoples of Brazil that Europeans call savage are more barbaric than Europe's own wars (Essays 1.31)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was a well-made head: a mind that can judge, not one stuffed with facts. Your line was well made, not full.

A pair of trousers. That's where today's essay lands. To get there, Montaigne travels a long way without leaving home. He starts with a man in his household who had lived a long time on the coast of Brazil, and who told him about the people there. He moves through what Europeans of his day said about those people. And he ends up back in France, in the middle of its own wars, carrying one question the whole way: who are the barbarians?
screen: `A JOKE ABOUT TROUSERS.` → `A REPORT FROM BRAZIL.` → `BACK TO FRANCE.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. The essay is called Of Cannibals. From what he's been told, Montaigne says, he finds nothing barbarous or savage in these people, except that each of us calls barbarous whatever isn't our own custom. Here the idea of custom gets teeth. Second, the mirror. He doesn't pretend the people he heard about were gentle. He describes them killing enemies in war and eating them. There is more barbarity, he says, in eating a man alive than dead: in tearing apart by torture a body that can still feel, and roasting it bit by bit. He says he has seen this done, not among old enemies but among neighbors and fellow citizens, under cover of piety and religion. He was describing his own country, in his own time. Third, the visitors. Some of these men came to France, and Montaigne records what struck them. They found it strange that so many tall, bearded, armed men would obey a child instead of choosing one of their own to lead. And they'd noticed some people stuffed with every good thing while others, whom they called their halves, begged at their doors, thin with hunger. They wondered why the hungry put up with it. Fourth, the trousers. The essay ends with a shrug in the reader's voice: not bad at all, but so what? They don't wear breeches. Montaigne lets his reader sneer, and the sneer gives the reader away. One honest note: he never went to Brazil. It all came secondhand, and he tells us whose hands.
screen: `OUR CUSTOM, THEIR BARBARISM.` · `TORTURE AMONG NEIGHBORS.` · `THE VISITORS' QUESTIONS.` · `THEY DON'T WEAR BREECHES.` · then, large: `WHO ARE THE BARBARIANS?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind an ordinary group you tend to call them, not the worst you can think of: people who vote, raise kids or eat dinner another way. Find one habit of theirs that looks odd to you, then turn it around the way Montaigne does: which habit of yours would look odd from their side of the table? Hold both for a while, without deciding who wins.
Who are the barbarians? Montaigne's question in Of Cannibals: each of us calls barbarous what isn't our own custom, and sometimes the cruelty is closer to home. Today's word.
Your line: who are the barbarians. Montaigne's question turns the mirror around before it points. That's day one thousand one hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take Of Cannibals as practice in turning a judgment around: before calling another people barbarous, look hard at what your own side does.

fork.setup: you're Montaigne. you've just written that the people of Brazil eat enemies killed in war. what comes next on the page?
options: a warning to readers about savages.
the cruelties you've seen neighbors do to each other in your own country's wars.
fork.reveal: he turns the lens around: tearing apart a living body by torture, done among fellow citizens under cover of religion, is more barbarous than eating the dead.

trapdoor: what you thought: Of Cannibals is a travel tale about a faraway people.
what it means: it's a mirror. the word barbarian tells you about the speaker's customs, and the cruelty he calls worse is at home.
what a scholar hears: the portrait of Brazil is secondhand and he says so; the eyewitness part of the essay is the cruelty of France's own religious wars.
recall: a try, a test, an attempt
guess: a question that turns the label barbarous back on ourselves
a history lesson about the tribes that invaded ancient Rome
a traveler's guide to the customs of the people of Brazil

chat.says: Why does Montaigne defend people who ate their enemies? Isn't that obviously barbaric?
options: He doesn't call them gentle; he says torturing living neighbors at home was worse.
He says they did it out of hunger, so no one should ever blame them for it.
He says those reports were made up, and those people never harmed anyone.
chat.meaning: Montaigne describes them killing and eating enemies, then says there's more barbarity in torturing a living body, as he'd seen among neighbors, under cover of piety.

Of Cannibals.meaning: Montaigne's essay on the people of Brazil and on barbarism

piety.meaning: religious devotion; here, used as a cover for cruelty

notes: All Montaigne is paraphrased; Cotton/Hazlitt is not on the validator's public-domain list and the writer did not rely on its exact wording.
Essay numbering follows the outline (1.31, the Villey/Pléiade numbering); Cotton's edition numbers it 1.30.
Original-language line 'chacun appelle barbarie ce qui n'est pas de son usage' is from memory of the French; confirm wording and pronunciation.
The visitors' 'child' is the young king; the script avoids naming him or giving the city or date of the meeting to keep within the claims rule.
The script calls the people 'the people of Brazil' as the outline does; Montaigne does not name the nation. Some modern readers identify them as Tupinambá; left out.
Days 1142–1151 were not on disk when this was written; the review uses the index line for day 1151.
